profile: Opens a paragraph on the previous paragraph's point, often restating it as a premise: 'If the signs are present and plain and yet we still pass them by, the fault is on our side.'; 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.'
Ends paragraphs on the point itself or on a plain lead-in to the next verse, not on a flourish: 'That machine is the soul.'; 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.'
Medium-length, plain declarative sentences, with short ones for emphasis: 'This claim is not contested.'; 'Most of us see only the lamp.'

Semicolons set two halves against each other; 'whereas' is rare: 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.'; 'Eyes and ears take in the surface of things, whereas inside a human being there should be something more'

Brings in sources with plain verbs ('reads', 'says', 'explains', 'insists'), one or two to a paragraph, and seldom parades them: 'Sheikh Bahmanpour reads it as being about what lies behind the senses.'

Explains a quotation or verse in its own words right after it: 'Cattle see and hear perfectly well, so the comparison cannot be about the senses.'; 'Four times in a row, the Qur'an makes the same point.'
Inclusive 'we/us' and an occasional 'Let's start with'; 'you' is almost never used, and there is no lecturing: 'Let's start with two claims.'; 'We have heard these verses many times'
Concrete, everyday images rather than grand abstraction: 'a person who sees a red light thinks of the danger it warns of, not of the colour and shape of the lamp'
Signposts the structure and cross-references other chapters briefly: 'That something and why it is worth developing, is the subject of this chapter.'; 'as Chapter One shows'
Moves the argument on in every paragraph, with numbered steps ('The first... The second...'): 'The second is that the problem can be solved.'
Never asks rhetorical questions, never ends on a tidy aphorism, never uses spoken filler; 'he says' appears at most once or twice in a paragraph

tells: Numbered steps ('The second gift... The third gift...') and a concern that picks up the last point ('None of this would matter to an ordinary reader if it were reserved for prophets. Surah al-Nisaʾ answers that concern.') match Author A, though the one-line paragraph after the Yunus verse is thin.

'Reason has a limit and Sheikh Bahmanpour says where it lies' mirrors 'The Qur'an says where it lies'; the concrete examples ('brown or square or useful') and the step to God at the end ('If this is true of the things around us, it is true far more of God') follow Author A's habit of building one step on the last.

The opening picks up the last point ('If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works'), the verse is explained in plain terms ('A heart trembles only at the mention of someone it has some experience of') and each paragraph leads into the next verse, all as Author A does.

Quotations are explained afterwards ('What the prayer asks to lose is the heart's love for the world, not the world itself'), in Author A's manner; the second paragraph partly restates the first, which weakens the match.

'Allah's light, the Sheikh says, is everywhere... It is not the case, he says... The light, the Sheikh says... The knowledge of the ʿurafaʾ, he says' — 'he says' used as filler four or five times; Author A attributes once and then speaks in its own voice.
'There is no hindrance on His side to pouring His knowledge and bounty upon us. His knowledge and bounty are all there' — says the same thing twice; Author A would make the point once.
'Chapter One reached the same conclusion by another road, when it placed the fault in the receiver.' — a closing look back that adds nothing; Author A ends on the point or leads into the next step.

'Requests this high raise a difficulty and Sheikh Bahmanpour states it himself' picks up the last paragraph as Author A does, and the closing gloss after the quotation ('The servant stands there because of need and the prayer gives no other reason for coming') matches.

Paragraphs link step by step ('Knowledge that analysis cannot produce has to come from somewhere else'), the hadith is explained right after it ('The hadith sets the two kinds of knowing side by side') and the ending leads into the next verse, all as Author A does.
'Imam Khomeini, in one of his talks, takes this familiarity for granted.' — loose link from a list of prayer times to 'familiarity'; Author A opens by picking up the last paragraph's actual point.

'Maliki Tabrizi... Imam Khomeini... Maliki Tabrizi... Imam Khomeini makes a narrower point' — a parade of scholars, one adding a side remark ('how to put God's relation to His creation into words') that does not move the argument on.

'The two positions answer different questions. The scholars speak of how far a reciter reaches; the Sheikh speaks of who may begin.' — a neat summary of positions, more academic in register than Author A.

'Murtada Mutahhari, the third, separates...' — scholars brought in as items in a list ('the third'), each in his own paragraph; Author A brings in a source to settle a step, not to fill out a roll-call.

'"For knowledge gives birth to action and action in turn brings knowledge". In his scheme, what is learned from the jurist begins the circle...' — the quotation is followed by a restatement of the sentence before it, not by an explanation that moves things on.
'through a veil removed and not a definition learned' — a balanced, aphoristic flourish; Author A states the distinction plainly.
'Those brought near to God, the ʿurafaʾ, know Him in the second way' — a paragraph that recaps what came before with no new step, and does not pick up Mutahhari's point.

Numbered requests ('The second request is love... The third request is nearness'), each quotation glossed afterwards, and the closing contrast ('For some of us... For some, God is present') put in plain 'us' terms, as Author A does.

'The great teachers of the Shia tradition make closely related points, each in his own words.' — a grand framing line that introduces a roll-call; Author A would bring in one source to support the step.
'his efforts are rendered invalid".' — the paragraph ends on the quotation with nothing after it; Author A explains a quotation in its own words.

'"...something other than God Himself" and he recalls Imam ʿAli (as) saying that he worshipped God not from fear...' — a long sentence that stacks a quotation and a second anecdote with 'and'; Author A would split it and say what it shows.

The concrete everyday opening ('no one has to be told that they are hungry'), inclusive 'we', the brief recap of Chapter One and 'Let's start with the two kinds of knowing' match how Author A opens Chapter One.

Short contrasting sentences ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment. The people of this verse fear Him with a fear that is not about punishment at all.'), a quotation glossed straight after it ('Other people look at the surface of the world...') and a numbered gift that leads into the verse all match Author A.

The opening formula ('These words come near the end of Duʿa Kumayl... The line asks God...') mirrors 'These words come from the Munajat Shaʿbaniyyah... The line asks God'; the chapter signposting and 'Let's start with' match Author A.
'ordinary people, he says... It is difficult, he says... yet he says... A human being, he says' — 'he says' used as filler four times in one paragraph; Author A attributes once and paraphrases.
'He means this as a statement of what we were made for.' — restates the point without moving it on; Author A would cut it.

'This is the case for pursuing ʿirfan. The Qur'an invites more than the minimum and what stands in the way...' — a summary paragraph that restates the chapter's conclusion; Author A stops on the point rather than recapping it.
